Beliefs propagate between agents node-to-node on a temporal multilayer graph. Edges can be cooperative, deceptive, trusted, or untrusted. To evaluate belief attribution, we use four metrics over the predicted graph versus the ground truth agent beliefs: final node accuracy, time-respecting node accuracy, temporal edge F1, and normalized structural distance. This paper contributes a benchmark and an evaluation framework for higher-order theory-of-mind reasoning.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7438399\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1108/sd-10-2016-0142\", \"title\": [\"Missing links in effective emerging markets strategies\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:sec>\\n<jats:title content-type=\\\"abstract-subheading\\\">Purpose</jats:title>\\n<jats:p>This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies.</jats:p>\\n</jats:sec>\\n<jats:sec>\\n<jats:title content-type=\\\"abstract-subheading\\\">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>\\n<jats:p>This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context.</jats:p>\\n</jats:sec>\\n<jats:sec>\\n<jats:title content-type=\\\"abstract-subheading\\\">Findings</jats:title>\\n<jats:p>Clayton Christenson in <jats:italic>The Innovator’s Dilemma</jats:italic> (1997) teaches us that many firms think they are too big to fail, or cannot fail, despite the fact they can see the competition coming from miles away. Whether it is hiding in plain sight, or they cannot see the wood for the trees, there seems to be a feeling in large corporations that while some organizations may be able to gain some competitive advantage, they will never be able to scale this up.
